titulo_es: Can / can't (ability and permission; Spanish “poder”, “saber hacer”)
descripcion_es: Ability, permission and requests with can and can't.
resumen: Can is a modal verb for ability (knowing how to do something or being able to do it), permission and requests. It has only one form for all persons and the next verb is an infinitive without to.

explicacion.texto: Can translates both Spanish “poder” and “saber” when we talk about ability: I can swim (Spanish “sé nadar”). It has no -s in the third person, it doesn't use do in questions and the next verb has no to.

filas: Yes, I can. / No, I can't.
Can you open the window, please?

items: The negative is written cannot (one word) or can't.
In the past: could / couldn't (I could swim when I was five).
Could you…? is a more polite request than Can you…?

ejemplos.frase: My grandfather can't use a computer.
ejemplos.traduccion: Mi abuelo no sabe usar un ordenador.

ejemplos.frase: She can play the piano very well.
ejemplos.traduccion: Sabe tocar el piano muy bien.

ejemplos.frase: Can you speak more slowly, please?

errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Can has no -s in the third person.
After can, the verb has no to.
Can makes questions by inversion, without do.
The negative is can't or cannot.

ejercicios.explicacion: This is can for ability, in its negative form can't (or cannot). The clue is the meaning: fish have no legs, so they don't have this ability. That is why it is “Fish can't walk”, with the same single form for the plural subject “fish”. Both negative forms in the unit are accepted: the short form “can't” and the full form “cannot”, written as one word.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Fish don't have this ability: can't.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The sentence would say that fish can walk, which is not true; you need the negative.
The full negative is normally written as one word, “cannot”; as two words it is only used in special cases for emphasis.
Can doesn't use do in the negative: we say “can't” or “cannot”.

ejercicios.explicacion: This is the most basic use of can: to talk about an ability someone has. The clue is the meaning of the sentence: flying is exactly what birds can do. That is why it is the affirmative form “can”, which is the same for all persons, also for a plural subject like “birds”. After it comes the verb “fly” without to.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The sentence would say that birds can't fly; here you need the affirmative.
Can never has -s, for any person, and certainly not with a plural subject.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the verb in brackets.
ejercicios.explicacion: The form rule in this unit applies: after can comes the infinitive without to and without -s. The clue is that “can” is already in the sentence, and the verb after it must be in its base form. Although the subject is “my daughter” (third person), the verb is “ride”, not “rides”: there is no -s on can or on the verb after it. Notice also that here can translates Spanish “saber” (ability).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: After can comes the infinitive without to.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mi hija sabe montar en bicicleta.

errores_previstos.explicacion: After can the verb has no -s, even with a third-person subject.
Can is followed by the infinitive without “to”.
After can you don't use the -ing form, but the base form “ride”.

ejercicios.frase: Can your brother cook? Yes, he ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule for short answers in the table applies: you repeat the modal, not the main verb or do. The clue is that the question uses “Can”: the short answer must use the same verb, “Yes, he can”. In affirmative short answers there is no contraction and you don't repeat “cook”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The short answer repeats the modal: Yes, he can.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The question uses can, not do/does; the short answer repeats can.
In the short answer the modal is enough: “Yes, he can”. Repeating the verb is not the short answer you need.
Can has no -s, not even with “he”.

ejercicios.explicacion: This is can for asking for permission, which the table lists as “Permission”: Can I…? The clue is the structure “___ I use your phone?”: the speaker is asking for permission to do something, and after it comes the infinitive without to “use”. With can, you make the question by inverting can and the subject, without do. “May I…?” would be more formal, but it is not one of the options.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To ask for permission: Can I…?

por_opcion.Can: Correct: “Can I…?” is the normal way to ask for permission.
por_opcion.Do: Incorrect: “Do I use your phone?” would ask if I usually use it, not ask for permission.
por_opcion.Am: Incorrect: “Am I use…” is not grammatical; “am” would need a past participle or an -ing form.

ejercicios.explicacion: The form rule applies: can + infinitive without to and without -s. The clue is that the subject “He” is third person, which makes you want to add -s, but after can the verb is always in its base form. That is why it is “He can speak three languages”. This is the most typical mistake with can, together with adding “to”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Can + infinitive without to and without -s.

por_opcion.speaks: Incorrect: after can the verb has no -s, even with the subject “he”.
por_opcion.to speak: Incorrect: can is followed by the infinitive without “to”.
por_opcion.speak: Correct: base form of the verb, without to or -s.

ejercicios.frase: Sorry, I ___ come to your party.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule for the negative of can applies: it is can't (or cannot), never with do or with “not” before it. The clue is “Sorry”, which tells you a negative is coming: the speaker can't go. That is why it is “I can't come to your party”. Can is a modal and doesn't need an auxiliary for the negative.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The negative of can is can't.
ejercicios.traduccion: Lo siento, no puedo ir a tu fiesta.

por_opcion.don't can: Incorrect: can doesn't use do for the negative; this copies normal verbs.
por_opcion.can't: Correct: the short negative form of can.
por_opcion.not can: Incorrect: “not” goes after can (“cannot”), never before it.

ejercicios.frase: When I was a child, I ___ swim.
ejercicios.explicacion: The list in this unit applies: in the past, ability is expressed with could / couldn't. The clue is “When I was a child”, which puts the sentence in the past. That is why it is “I could swim”. Could, like can, is followed by the infinitive without to and has only one form for all persons.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: In the past, ability is expressed with could.

por_opcion.can: Incorrect: it is present; with “When I was a child” you need the past.
por_opcion.could: Correct: the past of can for ability.
por_opcion.cans: Incorrect: this form doesn't exist; can never has -s.

ejercicios.enunciado: Change the sentence into a question.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule in this unit applies: can doesn't use do in questions; you just invert can and the subject. The clue is the affirmative sentence “She can drive”, which becomes a question when you put “Can” before “she”. The verb “drive” doesn't change and the sentence ends with a question mark.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Can doesn't use do/does to make questions: you just invert can and the subject.
With question intonation people understand it in conversation, but the correct question inverts the order: “Can she drive?”.
After can the verb has no -s: “drive”.

ejercicios.enunciado: Change the sentence into the negative (short form).
ejercicios.frase: We can see the sea from here.
respuestas: We can't see the sea from here.
We cannot see the sea from here.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule for the negative applies: can + not = can't (or cannot, one word). The clue is the instruction, which asks for the short negative form, although the full form is also accepted. Just change “can” to “can't” and don't change anything else: “We can't see the sea from here”. You don't add do.
ejercicios.traduccion: Desde aquí no se ve el mar.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We don't can see the sea from here.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Can doesn't make the negative with do: we say “can't” or “cannot”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We can't to see the sea from here.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After can't the verb has no “to”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We not can see the sea from here.
errores_previstos.explicacion: “Not” goes after can, making “cannot” or “can't”.

ejercicios.frase: My sister cans play the violin.
respuestas: My sister can play the violin.
ejercicios.explicacion: The form rule applies: can has only one form for all persons and has no -s in the third person. The clue is the subject “My sister”, which makes you want to add -s as with normal verbs. The correct sentence is “My sister can play the violin”. This is the first typical mistake in the unit.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mi hermana sabe tocar el violín.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My sister cans play the violin.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the sentence without the correction: can has no -s for any person.

errores_previstos.respuesta: My sister can plays the violin.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Moving the -s to the verb is also wrong: after can comes the base form “play”.

ejercicios.frase: Can you to help me with my bags?
respuestas: Can you help me with my bags?
ejercicios.explicacion: The form rule applies: can is followed by the infinitive without to. The clue is “to help”, which has an extra “to”. The correct question is “Can you help me with my bags?”, an informal request; with “Could you…?” it would be more polite, as the unit says.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Can is followed by the infinitive without to.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Can you to help me with my bags?
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the sentence without the correction: there is no “to” after can.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Do you can help me with my bags?
errores_previstos.explicacion: Can doesn't use do in questions; “Can you help…?” is enough.

ejercicios.enunciado: Put the words in order to make a question.
ejercicios.explicacion: The structure of questions with can applies: Can + subject + verb + complement, without do. The clue is the instruction, which asks for a question, so “can” goes first, followed by the subject “you”. Then come the verb without to “help” and the complement “me”. It is the most common request in English.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is a statement, not a question: to ask, can goes before the subject.
This copies the Spanish word order “¿me puedes ayudar?”: in English the complement “me” goes after the verb.

ejercicios.explicacion: The affirmative or negative structure with can applies: subject + can't + verb + complements. The clue is that “can't” already contains the negative, so you don't need do. After the verb “sing” comes the expression of manner “very well”, which always goes at the end, with “very” before “well”.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The adverb of manner “very well” goes after the verb, at the end of the sentence, not before the modal.
“Very” modifies “well” and goes before it: “very well”.

descripcion_larga_es: Can is the modal verb that translates both Spanish “poder” and “saber hacer algo” (I can swim, Spanish “sé nadar”), and it is also used to ask for permission and make requests. It is one of the first verbs you learn and it is used every day. It is difficult because it doesn't behave like a normal verb: it has no -s, it doesn't use do in questions or negatives and it is followed by the infinitive without to.

contexto.que_es: Can is a modal verb: one form for all persons, followed by a verb in the infinitive without to. It expresses ability (knowing how to do something or being able to do it), permission, requests and possibility. Its negative is cannot or can't and its past is could.
contexto.por_que_importa: It is used all the time to talk about what you can do, to ask for things and to ask for permission, from the first day of class. Mistakes with can (she cans, I can to go, do you can) are very noticeable and show a very basic level, so it is a good idea to make its form automatic from the start. To ask for something politely, you change to could.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: To say what someone knows how to do or is able to do (I can speak French), to ask for permission (Can I open the window?), to ask for a favour (Can you help me?) and to talk about possibilities (You can pay by card). Spanish speakers distinguish “poder” and “saber”; English uses can for both when it is about an ability, and you don't need to look for another verb for Spanish “saber nadar”.
